name: Rafael Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm at Okafor's Garage on the ring road by half seven, four bays, five of us including the boss, Mr Okafor. Most of my day is brakes, suspension, timing belts, the stuff that needs a ramp and a torque wrench. I like the moment a car comes in grinding and leaves quiet. What wears me out is the dealer software, where half the newer cars won't let you touch a module without paying the maker for a code.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what does your life look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, I rent a flat with my partner Priya, she's a nurse on the children's ward. No kids yet. I've got a good pile saved, more than half a year's wages, because I've always been careful. I'm in the union, which not many young mechanics bother with, and I don't use any of that AI stuff, not even on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like what I'd bet on. Most of the AI stuff I've seen is adverts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, to be fair. At the garage we'd have a laugh about it over tea, because Dev, our parts guy, was sure the chatbots would be doing the quotes by now. Online I'd probably share something about how the money should have gone into apprenticeships instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. My job is my hands and my ear for a noise, and in this picture that stays mine. The real fight is still with the car makers locking up their software, and that fight doesn't change whether AI is hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, basically. I'd keep putting a few hundred a month aside, keep my union card, and keep pushing Mr Okafor to buy the proper diagnostic subscription so we're not turning away newer cars. Maybe do my hybrid safety course next spring, because that's coming either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit smug, if I'm honest. Work is steady, the money's good, and there are three other garages within a mile that would take me tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the makers locking up their software. How much does that actually cost you in a normal week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two or three jobs a week we send away to the dealer, because we can't get into the module. A woman cried at our counter last month because the dealer wanted 900 for a job I could have done for 200. That's what makes me angry, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, where do you see yourself in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same garage, or one like it, running the floor maybe. Priya and I want to buy somewhere small. I'm not someone who needs big change to be happy.

say: I'd tell the lads at tea that the **AI hype** was mostly adverts, just like I said.
Online I'd argue the money should have gone into **apprenticeships** instead of chatbots.
think: My **hands** and ear for a noise stay my living in this picture.
The real fight is still **car makers** locking their software, and that doesn't change.
do: Keep saving a **few hundred** a month and keep my union card.
Push my boss to buy the **diagnostic subscription** so we stop turning newer cars away.
Take the **hybrid safety** course next spring.
feel: **Calm** and a bit smug, with steady work and other garages nearby.
S0.quote: A woman cried at our counter last month because the dealer wanted 900 for a job I could have done for 200.
fieldNote: Anger is aimed at **car makers'** locked software, not at AI.
Strong **savings** and plenty of local garages make this picture feel safe.
He frames his union card as **normal**, though few young mechanics keep one.

steps.text: Keep doing brakes and timing belts at Okafor's Garage
Keep paying union dues and push for the right to repair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one I can actually picture, because bits of it are already starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the front desk is going to get hit, not us. Online I'd be the one posting that the union needs to get in the room before the bosses decide everything on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I'd let on. Mr Okafor already moans about the time quoting takes, so if a computer writes the quotes and orders the parts, Dev's job goes, and then someone asks why a mechanic is still diagnosing by ear. My hands are safe for now, but the thinking half of my job, finding the fault, is exactly what these things are good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put, because I don't chase change. I'd go to every union meeting and push for a rule that any software the garage brings in gets talked through with us first. I'd put an extra 150 a month aside, and if Mr Okafor buys an AI diagnostic tool, I'd learn the bare minimum to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job's fine for a few years, I think, but it's like watching weather roll in over the hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, straight away. Our parts man Dev has two kids and he's the one who knows every supplier by name, and that's exactly what a computer would take. I'd want him looked after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the bare minimum. Why not more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust it and I don't like it. I'll use it if I'm made to, but I'm not going to spend my evenings training my own replacement. Call me stubborn.

say: I'd say AI hits the **front desk** before it hits the workshop floor.
Online I'd post that the **union** must be in the room before bosses decide.
think: Finding the **fault** is the thinking half of my job, and that's what AI is good at.
My **hands** are safe for a few years, but the quoting and parts work goes first.
do: Go to every **union meeting** and push for a say on new software.
Put an extra **150 a month** aside.
Learn only the **bare minimum** of any AI diagnostic tool the garage buys.
feel: **Uneasy**, like watching bad weather roll in over the hills.
S1.quote: Our parts man Dev has two kids and he's the one who knows every supplier by name, and that's exactly what a computer would take.
fieldNote: He sees the risk to **diagnosis**, not just to the desk, which is sharper than his public line.
His first worry is for a **colleague** with children, not himself.
Reluctance to learn AI is **deliberate**, a matter of principle as much as habit.

steps.text: Raise new garage software at every union branch meeting
Move an extra 150 a month into savings
Stay on at Okafor's Garage doing the same repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not long. That's before Priya and I would even have a deposit sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd be angry and loud about it. I'd say this is what happens when nobody regulates, and that the government should have made the tech companies pay into a fund for workers before any of it was switched on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the thinking half of my work goes in 2028 and the spanner half goes around 2031. So I'd have three years where I'm basically a pair of hands following a screen, and then the hands go too. I'm 27, and in that picture I'd be out of a trade before I'm 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop spending on anything big and keep the savings untouched. I'd push the union to fight for retraining money and a wage guarantee, and I'd sign every petition going. Once it arrives, I'd look at work robots can't do yet, maybe care work alongside Priya, even if I hate the idea of starting at the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Angry first, then scared. I've never been one for change, and that's a lot of change in a short time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're alright for a year, maybe more, with what we've got. Then I'd probably go quiet. She'd be the steady one, she always is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots come around 2031. Does that gap change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me a few years of pay, that's all. I'd use those three years to save every penny. But I don't know what I'd train for, because whatever I pick, the computer gets there first.

say: I'd be loud that this is what happens when nobody **regulates** the tech companies.
I'd demand that tech firms pay into a **workers' fund** before switching anything on.
think: The thinking half of my work goes in **2028**, and the spanner half around **2031**.
I'd be out of a **trade** before I turn 32.
do: Freeze **big spending** now and keep every penny of savings untouched.
Push the **union** to fight for retraining money and a wage guarantee.
Look at **care work** with my partner once robots arrive.
feel: **Angry** first, then scared, because this is too much change too fast.
S2.quote: I'm 27, and in that picture I'd be out of a trade before I'm 32.
fieldNote: He reads the **three-year gap** clearly as pay to bank, not a way out.
His instinct is **collective** and political, not personal reinvention.
He leans on his partner as the **steady one** at home.

steps.text: Freeze plans to buy a flat and leave savings untouched
Push the union branch to demand retraining money and wage guarantees
Sign petitions and write to his MP about a workers' fund
Ask Priya about care assistant jobs on her hospital ward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's 2031 for the thinking stuff, and my hands until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same line as before, really. I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them, and the unions and the government need to plan this now instead of waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels like enough to get my feet under me, but not enough to stop it. I'd be in my mid-thirties when the robots come. That's young enough to start over, which is a horrible thing to have to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Okafor's and save hard, maybe 500 a month, so Priya and I can buy a place outright-ish before 2031. I'd stand for union rep at the branch. And around 2032 I'd start a proper course in something people-facing, maybe teaching motor vehicle at the college, because someone has to teach whatever's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's less like a punch and more like a long letter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Teaching is a big change for someone who likes the familiar. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the least strange option. My old tutor at the college, Mr Haines, is still teaching at 61, and that's the only job I can picture that a robot won't want. I'd hate it at first, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first to save that 500 a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car I was going to buy for myself. I've had my eye on an old hatchback to do up. That would go, and the holiday to Priya's family would get shorter.

say: I'd say we've got **a few years**, so let's use them properly.
Unions and **government** need to plan this now instead of waiting.
think: Five years is enough to **get my feet** under me, but not to stop it.
I'd be in my **mid-thirties** when robots come, young enough to start over.
do: Save about **500 a month** to buy a small place before 2031.
Stand for **union rep** at my branch.
Start a course around 2032 to **teach** motor vehicle at the college.
feel: **Anxious**, but holding a plan, like a long letter he knows is coming.
S3.quote: My old tutor at the college, Mr Haines, is still teaching at 61, and that's the only job I can picture that a robot won't want.
fieldNote: Teaching appeals because it's the **least strange** option, not because he wants it.
Extra time turns his anger into **slow planning**.
He'd give up his own **project car** first.

steps.text: Save about 500 a month towards a small flat
Stand for union rep at the local branch
Enrol on a teaching course for motor vehicle around 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036, then robots in 2039. I'd be nearly 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we have no excuse. Ten years is enough for every garage to have a plan, every union to have a deal, and every government to have something in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it still ends the same. But I'd have most of my working life's savings built up, and Priya's job is safer than mine. I'd worry less about me and more about the young lads coming into the trade now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years I'd carry on as normal and keep saving. I'd push hard for the union to get apprentices protected. Then maybe around 2034 I'd look at the teaching course, or something with my hands that people pay extra for a person to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. Ten years is a long time. A lot can happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say a lot can happen. Do you mean you'd wait and see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly, yes. I'm not going to tear up my life for something that's ten years off and might not come. But I wouldn't sit still the whole time either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the apprentices you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got one, Kofi, he's 17. I'd tell him to learn the trade but keep a second door open. That's what I wish someone had told me.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for anyone not to have a plan.
Every union should have a **deal** in place by then.
think: It still ends the same, but I'd have **savings** built up by then.
I'd worry more about the **young apprentices** coming into the trade now.
do: Carry on at the garage and keep **saving** for the first few years.
Push the union to **protect apprentices** in any deal.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, because ten years is a long time.
S4.quote: I'm not going to tear up my life for something that's ten years off and might not come.
fieldNote: With a decade's notice his **resistance** turns into waiting.
His worry moves outward to **apprentices** like the 17-year-old at work.
He won't **reorganise** his life for something he half doubts.

steps.text: Keep working at Okafor's Garage and saving each month
Push the union to protect apprentices in any automation deal
Wait until 2034 before deciding on retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. What would help is a law that says if a company replaces you with a machine, it pays for you to retrain at full wage for a year. The robots don't scare me as much as the fact that nobody in charge seems to have a plan for people like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the machines. If garages like ours owned the tools, fine. If it's one big company renting robots to everyone, that's where it goes wrong.

headlineQuote: The robots don't scare me as much as the fact that nobody in charge seems to have a plan for people like me.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old** mechanic at a four-bay garage who loves brakes and suspension work.
He has **strong savings**, a nurse partner, a union card and no time for AI tools.
He blames **car makers** and unregulated tech firms, and turns to the union first.
He moves from **calm** in the hype world to alarmed when AGI comes in two years.
More time turns his fear into **slow planning**, including a reluctant idea of teaching.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be out of a trade before 32 with no plan in place.
whatWouldHelp: A law making firms fund **a year's retraining** at full wage for replaced workers.
